paragraphs: Compressing a neural network becomes especially delicate when some classes have many examples and others have very few. Parameters that appear less important overall may still matter for those rare classes. This paper introduces Long-Tailed Adaptive Pruner, or LTAP, to make pruning decisions sensitive to that imbalance while pursuing a smaller, more efficient model.

LTAP scores parameter importance along multiple dimensions and dynamically adjusts the weights used in those scores. This lets it adapt which parameters receive priority for removal according to their importance for different classes. Protecting parameters needed by tail classes is central to the approach: compression decisions explicitly account for the parts of the classification problem that have fewer examples.

The reported experiments show LTAP outperforming existing methods across several long-tailed datasets while balancing compression, computation, and classification accuracy. The practical contribution is a way to connect efficiency decisions with class-specific needs. Its findings support treating class imbalance as part of the pruning problem itself, since maintaining performance requires attention to which capabilities survive compression.
icml-2025-balancing-model-efficiency-and.tldr: LTAP adapts parameter pruning to protect rare classes while improving model efficiency and preserving classification performance.

paragraphs: Protein sequences and fluorescence microscopy images describe different aspects of the same biological system. A sequence specifies a protein's amino acid composition, while microscopy helps researchers characterize its cellular role. CELL-Diff connects these forms of information through a unified diffusion model designed to translate between sequences and their corresponding protein images.

In the sequence-to-image direction, the model takes both a protein sequence and reference images describing cell morphology. These inputs guide the generation of a corresponding protein image. In the reverse direction, it takes a protein image and produces protein sequences. A transformer-based network implements the shared framework, allowing the two transformation directions to be addressed within one model.

The researchers train CELL-Diff using the Human Protein Atlas dataset and then fine-tune it on OpenCell. Their experiments report higher-fidelity protein image generation than existing methods. This result supports its use for investigating where proteins localize within cells and how they interact. The stated comparative finding concerns image generation, while bidirectional sequence-image transformation is the broader capability introduced by the framework.
icml-2025-bridging-protein-sequences-and.tldr: CELL-Diff translates between protein sequences and microscopy images, with experiments showing improved protein image fidelity.

paragraphs: Deep binary neural networks offer lightweight computation for settings with limited resources, but environmental noise can undermine their predictions. The paper examines this issue in applications motivated by bio-electrical signal classification and ultrasound-assisted diagnosis, where patient movement and device noise can affect the input. Its central question is whether a trained binary network can remain robust during inference.

The analysis identifies binary weights and their scaling factors as sources of vulnerability. Guided by theoretical results, the authors constrain both using L1-infinite norms. These constraints yield a tighter upper bound than the compared state-of-the-art methods, providing a mathematical basis for the proposed approach to noise robustness.

Experiments on bio-electrical and image classification datasets show the method outperforming the state-of-the-art comparison. Visualizations also show minimal noise perturbations around the edges of feature maps under the proposed approach. Together, these findings connect an identified source of sensitivity to a targeted intervention and empirical improvements. They support paying attention to how binary weights are scaled when designing efficient models for noisy inputs.
icml-2025-can-dbnns-robust-to-environmen.tldr: Constraining binary weights and scaling factors improves deep binary networks' resistance to environmental noise in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Evaluating every large vision-language model on every relevant task can be expensive. This paper asks whether scores already collected for some model-task combinations can help predict the missing ones. It organizes the available evidence into a sparse matrix, with models along one dimension, datasets along the other, and measured performance in the filled entries.

The proposed framework uses probabilistic matrix factorization to infer missing scores from patterns in that matrix. Markov chain Monte Carlo supplies both predictions and estimates of their uncertainty. That uncertainty has a practical role: evaluators can prioritize untested tasks whose predicted scores are less certain, adding measurements that help reduce subsequent prediction errors.

The authors also modify the factorization approach for cases where very few scores are available. Experiments support the accuracy of the inferred scores, the usefulness of uncertainty for ordering evaluations, and the improvements under sparse observations. The contribution therefore combines performance estimation with a strategy for deciding what to measure next, making existing evaluation results more useful for planning further evaluations.
icml-2025-can-we-predict-performance-of-.tldr: Probabilistic matrix completion predicts missing vision-language evaluation scores and uses uncertainty to prioritize further testing.

paragraphs: Maximum likelihood training encourages visual generative models to cover the data distribution broadly, which can constrain image quality when model capacity is limited. Direct Discriminative Optimization, or DDO, introduces a fine-tuning objective that combines likelihood-based generation with GAN-style discrimination. It uses reverse KL and negative examples generated by the model itself to refine an already trained generator.

The discriminator is represented implicitly through the likelihood ratio between the model being updated and a fixed reference model. This avoids jointly training separate generator and discriminator networks. Refinement can proceed through repeated self-play rounds, each requiring less than 1% of the pretraining epochs according to the abstract.

For the EDM diffusion model, the reported FID scores improve from 1.79 to 1.30 on CIFAR-10, from 1.58 to 0.97 on ImageNet-64, and from 1.96 to 1.26 on ImageNet at 512-by-512 resolution, without guidance. DDO also improves visual autoregressive models with and without classifier-free guidance. These findings demonstrate gains across both diffusion and autoregressive generation using the proposed fine-tuning framework.
icml-2025-direct-discriminative-optimiza.tldr: DDO improves visual generation by fine-tuning likelihood-based models with an implicit discriminator and self-generated negative examples.

paragraphs: Visual tokenization compresses images into compact representations that generative models can work with more efficiently. A conventional autoencoder learns an encoder for compression and a decoder that reconstructs an image in one step. Epsilon-VAE changes the reconstruction stage by treating decoding as an iterative denoising problem.

Its encoder still supplies a compressed latent representation, but a diffusion process replaces the conventional decoder. Starting from noise, this process repeatedly refines an image under guidance from the encoded information. This connects the compressed representation to a sequence of reconstruction steps, giving the decoder an iterative route to recover the original visual content.

The paper evaluates both reconstruction quality through rFID and downstream generation quality through FID. It reports a 22% improvement in downstream generation quality at the same compression rates, or a 2.3-fold inference speedup when increasing compression. These are two reported ways of using the approach's improved reconstruction capability. The findings show that changing how compressed information is decoded can affect both the quality and efficiency of the wider generation pipeline.
icml-2025-epsilon-vae-denoising-as-visua.tldr: Epsilon-VAE uses diffusion-based iterative decoding to improve visual reconstruction and downstream generation or enable faster inference through greater compression.

paragraphs: Physical systems on irregular grids can contain both detailed local interactions and effects spanning large distances. Computing attention between every pair of nodes becomes expensive because the number of pairs grows quadratically. Erwin addresses this scaling problem with a hierarchical transformer inspired by tree-based methods from computational many-body physics.

The model organizes nodes using a ball tree and computes attention in parallel inside fixed-size local neighborhoods. This arrangement enables linear-time attention. To connect information across scales, Erwin progressively coarsens and refines the tree representation. A cross-ball interaction mechanism also exchanges information between neighborhoods, helping the model capture global features alongside fine local detail.

Experiments cover cosmology, molecular dynamics, and particle fluid dynamics. Across these evaluated domains, Erwin consistently exceeds the compared baselines in both accuracy and computational efficiency. The significance is that its efficiency mechanism also organizes how information moves through the system: local attention handles nearby structure, while the hierarchy and cross-ball exchanges support broader interactions. The reported results support this combination for large physical learning problems.
icml-2025-erwin-a-tree-based-hierarchica.tldr: Erwin combines local attention with a tree hierarchy to model large physical systems efficiently while capturing interactions across scales.

paragraphs: Reducing the bits used to store language-model weights can save memory, but practical speed depends on how those weights are processed. The paper identifies two obstacles: inefficient implementations that must dequantize weights for mixed-precision matrix multiplication, and uniform quantization that poorly represents weight distributions. GANQ addresses representation quality and GPU execution together.

GANQ is a post-training, non-uniform quantization framework that operates layer by layer. Its training-free optimization adapts to the GPU while reducing each layer's quantization error. The resulting representation is designed for hardware-efficient mixed-precision matrix multiplication based on lookup tables, tying the choice of quantization to the computation used during inference.

Experiments with 3-bit and 4-bit weights show a smaller perplexity gap from the FP16 baseline than the compared state-of-the-art methods. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090, the quantized models reach up to 2.57 times the baseline speed. These results connect better preservation of model behavior with measured hardware efficiency, with the stated speedup applying to the reported deployment setting.
icml-2025-ganq-gpu-adaptive-non-uniform-.tldr: GANQ combines GPU-adaptive non-uniform quantization with lookup-table computation to improve low-bit language-model quality and inference speed.

paragraphs: GraphGPT applies generative pretraining to graph learning by first making graphs usable as token sequences. Its Graph Eulerian Transformer converts a graph or sampled subgraph into tokens describing nodes, edges, and attributes. The conversion uses Eulerian paths and is reversible, preserving the graph information represented by the sequence.

This representation lets the method use a standard transformer encoder or decoder. Pretraining uses either next-token prediction or scheduled masked-token prediction, learning from the graph sequences without requiring task-specific labels at that stage. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned for predictions about entire graphs, individual edges, or individual nodes.

On multiple large-scale Open Graph Benchmark datasets, GraphGPT matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong reported results for molecular property prediction on PCQM4Mv2 and protein interactions on ogbl-ppa. The authors also scale it to two billion parameters while continuing to obtain performance gains. This is the main scaling result: their graph representation and generative training approach support a substantially larger model with continued empirical benefit.
icml-2025-graphgpt-generative-pre-traine.tldr: GraphGPT reversibly converts graphs into token sequences, enabling generative transformer pretraining and continued performance gains at two billion parameters.

paragraphs: Hierarchical robot policies divide work between a high-level agent that handles longer-horizon reasoning and a low-level agent that performs precise control. This paper focuses on the interface connecting those agents. It also addresses the tendency of existing hierarchical methods to overlook domain symmetries, which the abstract links to needing extensive demonstrations for robust behavior.

The proposed Hierarchical Equivariant Policy uses frame transfer: the high-level agent produces a coordinate frame that the low-level agent uses to interpret its control problem. That interface supplies a strong structural bias while preserving flexibility. The framework additionally incorporates domain symmetries at both levels, and the authors theoretically establish equivariance of the overall system.

Equivariance means that the policy's behavior transforms consistently with the symmetries incorporated into its design. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on complex manipulation tasks, with significant gains in simulation and real-world settings. The contribution connects a concrete communication mechanism between hierarchy levels with a system-wide symmetry property, and evaluates that combination in robotic control.
icml-2025-hierarchical-equivariant-polic.tldr: HEP passes coordinate frames between policy levels and incorporates symmetry to improve hierarchical robotic manipulation.

paragraphs: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, or KANs, replace conventional neural-network weights with learnable functions of one variable. This gives them potential advantages for function approximation and interpretability, but their larger number of trainable parameters can increase memory demands and training costs. MetaKANs targets that cost while retaining the underlying KAN approach.

The method uses a smaller meta-learner to generate the KAN's weights. The KAN and this weight-generating model are trained together through an end-to-end differentiable process. This changes how the KAN's parameters are obtained and allows the system to reduce the number of parameters that must be directly trained.

Experiments span symbolic regression, partial differential equation solving, and image classification. The authors report comparable or better performance, substantially fewer trainable parameters, improved memory usage, and promising interpretability. The findings support weight generation as an alternative training technique for KANs across several kinds of tasks. They also narrow the training-cost gap with conventional multilayer perceptrons, making the KAN design more scalable without claiming that the gap disappears entirely.
icml-2025-improving-memory-efficiency-fo.tldr: MetaKANs uses a smaller weight-generating model to reduce KAN training memory and parameter costs while maintaining or improving performance.

paragraphs: KL regularization is used in reinforcement learning from human feedback, but its theoretical effect on learning efficiency has been less clear than its empirical usefulness. This paper studies that distinction through regret, which tracks accumulated shortfall in decision quality. It develops an online contextual bandit algorithm built around optimistic reward estimates and a KL-regularized objective.

The analysis uses the favorable optimization landscape created by regularization together with those optimistic estimates. The resulting regret bound grows logarithmically with the number of rounds. Its stated form is O(η log(N_R T) d_R), where η is the regularization parameter, N_R is the size of the reward function class, T counts rounds, and d_R describes that class's complexity.

The authors then extend the algorithm and analysis to reinforcement learning using a new decomposition across transition steps, obtaining a similar logarithmic bound. The contribution is a theoretical account of how regularization and exploration can work together. The logarithmic guarantee belongs to the proposed algorithms and their analysis, providing a specific explanation for efficiency gains rather than an empirical claim about every RLHF procedure.
icml-2025-logarithmic-regret-for-online-.tldr: The paper derives logarithmic regret bounds for proposed optimism-based algorithms in KL-regularized contextual bandits and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Model immunization aims to make a pretrained model difficult to fine-tune for harmful tasks while preserving usefulness on non-harmful tasks. Earlier work had demonstrated empirical examples, but the conditions under which immunization is possible remained unclear. This paper develops a mathematical framework to make that question more precise for linear models.

The framework centers on the condition number of a Hessian matrix, a quantity describing the curvature of an optimization problem. It uses this perspective to analyze immunization and then derives an algorithm with regularization terms that control the condition numbers resulting from pretraining. The method therefore makes properties of later optimization an explicit concern during the initial training stage.

Experiments demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness on both linear models and nonlinear deep networks. The distinction between these results matters: the stated analytical framework concerns linear models, while the deep-network evidence is empirical. Together, they provide a theoretical lens and a practical intervention for making harmful adaptation harder while retaining useful capabilities, matching the paper's objective of resistance to harmful fine-tuning.
icml-2025-model-immunization-from-a-cond.tldr: A Hessian-based framework guides pretraining regularization intended to resist harmful fine-tuning while preserving useful model behavior.

paragraphs: Low-rank pruning can compress language models in a GPU-compatible form, but it can also substantially degrade model quality. This paper separates two opportunities: storing an existing low-rank representation more compactly and reducing the errors introduced by pruning. Pivoting Factorization, or PIFA, addresses the first through a lossless representation of low-rank structure.

PIFA identifies linearly independent pivot rows and expresses other rows as combinations of those pivots. This removes redundant information from the representation. At a rank equal to half the dimension, the authors report 24.2% additional memory savings and 24.6% faster inference over low-rank layers. Losslessness applies to representing the low-rank object; the paper separately addresses degradation caused by obtaining that object through pruning.

For that second problem, a retraining-free reconstruction method minimizes error accumulation. Combining reconstruction with PIFA produces MPIFA, which reportedly outperforms existing low-rank pruning methods and reaches performance comparable to semi-structured pruning. It also exceeds semi-structured pruning in GPU efficiency and compatibility in the reported comparisons, linking quality recovery with compact execution.
icml-2025-pivoting-factorization-a-compa.tldr: MPIFA combines lossless compaction of low-rank representations with retraining-free reconstruction to improve compressed language-model efficiency and quality.

paragraphs: Planning agents often use learned generators to propose desirable or expected future states. If a generator proposes an infeasible target, the agent may plan around something it cannot achieve. This paper first investigates kinds of infeasible targets and then introduces a learned evaluator that identifies and rejects them before they drive delusional behavior.

The evaluator combines an off-policy-compatible learning rule, a distributional architecture, and data augmentation through hindsight relabeling. The authors choose this combination to make the evaluator robust and avoid reproducing the generator's mistaken expectations. It learns from the agent's interactions with its environment and from the targets that the generator proposes.

A useful feature is that the evaluator can attach to an existing planning agent without changing either the agent or its generator. Controlled experiments show significant reductions in delusional behavior and improved performance across different existing agents. These findings support feasibility assessment as a practical addition to model-based target generation: the system gains a learned check on proposed destinations while retaining the original planning machinery.
icml-2025-rejecting-hallucinated-state-t.tldr: A learned feasibility evaluator filters impossible planning targets and reduces delusional behavior across several tested agents.

paragraphs: Learning the ground-state properties of quantum systems is computationally demanding, and both traditional machine learning and deep learning have been proposed for the job. This paper asks what deep learning specifically contributes. Its starting concern is that earlier comparisons used different or impractical quantum resources to construct datasets, making the methods difficult to assess fairly.

The authors benchmark the two model families while enforcing equivalent quantum resource usage. Their study covers three families of Hamiltonians, three ground-state learning tasks, and systems as large as 127 qubits. This shared resource constraint is central to the comparison because it makes the available quantum information a controlled part of the evaluation.

Traditional machine-learning models often match or exceed deep-learning performance across the tested tasks. A randomization test also finds that measurement input features have little effect on the deep models' predictions. These results question the necessity of current deep-learning approaches in many of the examined scenarios. They support closer scrutiny of what information the models use and what benefit their added complexity provides under comparable resources.
icml-2025-rethink-the-role-of-deep-learn.tldr: Under matched quantum resources, traditional machine learning often matches or exceeds deep learning on the studied ground-state prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Static layer pruning treats a language model's computation too uniformly to capture two differences emphasized by this paper: tokens have different contextual needs, and self-attention and MLP components serve different functions. SkipGPT makes pruning responsive to both. Its goal is to allocate computation according to the token being processed and the component doing the work.

The framework uses global token-aware routing to prioritize critical tokens and separate pruning policies for attention and MLP components. Training proceeds in two stages. First, soft parameterization lets the routing strategies develop without committing too early to pruning decisions. Then parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning helps recover performance affected by layer removal.

The reported experiments remove more than 40% of model parameters while matching or exceeding the original dense model's performance across benchmarks. That result supports combining adaptive routing with component-specific decisions and subsequent recovery training. The central contribution is an efficiency strategy that recognizes variation within inference, with the reported quality preservation demonstrated on the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2025-skipgpt-each-token-is-one-of-a.tldr: SkipGPT combines token-aware routing and separate component pruning policies to remove over 40% of parameters while preserving benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Sparse Spectral Training, or SST, targets the memory demands of neural-network pretraining. The paper argues that existing memory-saving approaches can restrict learning through low-rank structure or encounter optimization difficulties. SST works with a matrix's spectral components, separating its singular values from its singular vectors to decide which parts receive updates.

The method updates every singular value while updating only selected singular vectors. Selection uses multinomial sampling weighted by the magnitude of the singular values. Singular value decomposition initializes and periodically reinitializes the low-rank parameters. The authors use these steps to reduce distortion relative to full-rank training compared with other low-rank methods.

Tests on Euclidean and hyperbolic networks show stronger results than existing memory-reduction training methods and performance comparable to full-rank training in various cases. On LLaMA-1.3B, SST trains 18.7% as many parameters as full-rank training, using a rank equal to 6% of the embedding dimension. In that setting, it closes 97.4% of the perplexity gap between other low-rank approaches and full-rank training, supporting its usefulness for parameter-efficient pretraining.
icml-2025-sparse-spectral-training-and-i.tldr: SST updates all singular values and selected singular vectors to reduce training memory while approaching full-rank performance in reported settings.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation seeks a compact training dataset that retains the usefulness of a much larger one. Diffusion models can generate distilled images, but image-generation ability alone does not ensure that those images represent the source distribution well. This paper investigates inaccurate distribution matching, deviations introduced by random noise, and separate sampling in existing diffusion-based approaches.

Its proposed framework, D3HR, uses DDIM inversion to map the full dataset's latent representations into a domain that more closely follows a Gaussian distribution. The mapping is designed to preserve information and structural consistency while producing representative latents for the compact dataset. An efficient sampling scheme further aligns those representative latents with the Gaussian domain.

Experiments show higher accuracy than state-of-the-art dataset-distillation baselines across different model architectures. The contribution is therefore about organizing generation around representativeness: both the latent transformation and the sampling procedure work toward retaining the larger dataset's useful structure. The cross-architecture findings indicate that the resulting distilled data benefits multiple evaluated model designs.
icml-2025-taming-diffusion-for-dataset-d.tldr: D3HR improves diffusion-based dataset distillation by preserving representative latent structure and aligning its sampling with a Gaussian domain.

paragraphs: A graph neural network can lose accuracy when the graphs encountered at deployment differ from those used for training. Test-time adaptation attempts to respond using only the available test data. ASSESS addresses this setting without access to the original training graphs, combining reliable test-graph selection with information retained in the trained model.

Its selection mechanism uses fine-grained subgraph mutual information to adaptively identify reliable test graphs. The method also constructs semantic prototypes from the pretrained model. These prototypes serve as prior knowledge about the unavailable training graphs, and the method updates the corresponding posterior using unlabeled test graphs.

This combination gives adaptation two sources of guidance: local structural evidence for selecting test examples and model-derived semantic information for supervision. The authors provide a theoretical analysis and report effectiveness against various baselines in extensive experiments. The contribution is a graph-specific adaptation strategy that uses the deployed model's existing knowledge together with new unlabeled data, addressing distribution shifts under the explicit constraint that training data cannot be accessed.
icml-2025-test-time-adaptation-on-graphs.tldr: ASSESS adapts graph models using reliable test-graph selection and model-derived prototypes without accessing original training data.

paragraphs: This paper frames graph test-time adaptation as a search over the data presented to a trained graph neural network. The proposed problem, test-time graph neural dataset search, learns a parameterized distribution of test graphs to improve inference on unseen examples. The motivation is to increase the flexibility and generalization of existing approaches that adapt graph data.

PGNDS implements this idea through generative projection. A dual conditional diffusion module, guided by the trained GNN, maps the unseen test distribution toward the known training distribution. A dynamic search then selects expressive test graphs from the generative sampling space. Finally, ensemble inference combines information from the original graphs and their adapted versions.

The three modules connect distribution adjustment, candidate selection, and final prediction. Preserving the original graphs within the ensemble lets the prediction draw on both the initial input and the generated adaptations. Experiments on real-world graphs report improved test-time GNN inference relative to the compared approaches, supporting generative dataset search as a way to adapt the inputs used by a well-trained model.
icml-2025-test-time-graph-neural-dataset.tldr: PGNDS generates and searches adapted test graphs, then combines them with original graphs to improve GNN inference.

paragraphs: Attribution methods explain a model's prediction by assigning contributions to input variables, sometimes grouping variables into coalitions. The paper examines how those groups should be formed. Existing methods commonly assume a partition has already been chosen, leaving open whether the resulting groups provide a meaningful explanation of the model's behavior.

The authors focus on attribution conflicts: a group's assigned contribution can differ from the sum of the contributions assigned to its individual members. They analyze how AND-OR interactions produce these discrepancies and extend Shapley-value attribution to a new measure for variable coalitions. Their theory identifies specific interactions responsible for conflicts, and they propose three metrics for evaluating coalition faithfulness.

Experiments span synthetic data, natural language processing, image classification, and Go. The reported results support practical applicability and agreement with human intuition. The contribution makes grouping itself part of the explanation problem, providing tools to assess whether a coalition's attribution faithfully reflects the interactions among its members. This helps interpret discrepancies between explanations given at individual-variable and group levels.
icml-2025-towards-attributions-of-input-.tldr: The paper extends Shapley attribution to variable coalitions and analyzes when interactions make group and individual explanations disagree.

paragraphs: Synthetic context extension fine-tunes language models on artificially constructed long inputs to reduce the cost of learning long-context capabilities. This paper investigates how that training supports later retrieval and reasoning. It studies three tasks while varying both the realism of the information to retrieve and the diversity of its surrounding context.

The training data ranges from language-model-generated documents to templated relations and symbolic datasets. Across these settings, the authors examine retrieval heads, attention components associated with retrieving relevant information. They find substantial overlap between the retrieval heads learned from synthetic data and those learned from real data, suggesting a shared feature of the attention computation.

Models trained on synthetic data still underperform models trained on real data in the reported study. However, the recall of learned retrieval heads correlates strongly with downstream performance, helping the authors interpret and predict differences between training settings. This connects a measurable internal feature to the effectiveness of context-extension data and offers a basis for investigating how synthetic training examples might better support real-world long-context capabilities.
icml-2025-understanding-synthetic-contex.tldr: Synthetic and real long-context training develop overlapping retrieval heads, whose recall strongly correlates with downstream performance.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models can improve decision transformers used in offline reinforcement learning, but the source of that transferred benefit is not obvious. This paper analyzes individual attention heads and identifies Markov heads that concentrate strongly on the most recent input token. The authors link these heads to good performance in short-term environments and difficulties beyond them.

The paper also proves that retraining the embedding layer or fine-tuning cannot change the extreme attention behavior it analyzes. This finding motivates changing the attention mechanism itself. The proposed GPT-DTMA equips a pretrained decision transformer with a Mixture of Attention, allowing adaptive learning to accommodate different attention requirements during fine-tuning.

Experiments show better performance than baselines in short-term environments and a substantial reduction in the performance gap affecting pretrained language models in long-term scenarios. The results also support the theoretical findings. The contribution connects an internal attention pattern to the circumstances in which transfer helps, then introduces an architectural response intended to make the transferred model useful across a broader range of temporal demands.
icml-2025-unveiling-markov-heads-in-pret.tldr: GPT-DTMA adds adaptive mixtures of attention to address pretrained heads that overemphasize the latest token in offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether small models can undermine the safety behavior of a much larger aligned language model during inference. Its motivation is the computational cost of existing jailbreak methods. The proposed weak-to-strong attack builds on the authors' observation that aligned and jailbroken models differ in their initial decoding distributions.

At a high level, the method uses a smaller safe model and a smaller unsafe model to alter a larger safe model's decoding probabilities. The intervention therefore acts on generation behavior at inference time. The central security finding is that information from smaller models can be sufficient to induce harmful generation from a substantially larger aligned model.

The authors evaluate five open-source language models from three organizations and report misalignment rates above 99% on two datasets with one forward pass per example. Those figures describe the reported evaluation settings. The paper also proposes an initial defense, while explicitly acknowledging that stronger defenses remain challenging. Its contribution is to expose an efficient attack pathway and demonstrate that alignment can be vulnerable to externally modified decoding.
icml-2025-weak-to-strong-jailbreaking-on.tldr: The study shows that smaller models can steer a larger aligned model toward harmful outputs by modifying inference-time decoding probabilities.
